extracted.intended_audience: photographers, photographic students, craftsmen in glass painting, and laboratory technicians performing small-scale chemical preparations
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, step-by-step guidance for making and handling gelatine photographic emulsions and coating plates (with adjacent instructions for vitrifiable-picture-on-glass technique and a laboratory method for producing hydrogen sulphide). Emphasis is on materials, proportions, temperatures, timings, and practical tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of silver nitrate
rubrics_metrics.description: Silver nitrate supplied in three principal forms: ordinary crystallized salt (contains free acid and impurities), fused nitrate or 'lunar caustic' (alkaline to test paper), and recrystallized silver nitrate (colorless, neutral, purer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For inexperienced workers use recrystallized silver nitrate. Prepare a solution of recrystallized silver nitrate in distilled water containing 1¼ ounces of the salt in every 12 ounces of solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of soluble bromide (avoid ammonium bromide)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various bromides may be used (ammonium, potassium, barium, zinc), but ammonium bromide is unstable, becomes acidic on keeping, varies in bromine percentage, and has a destructive action on gelatine producing pink fog and frilling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer potassium bromide: it is stable, obtainable pure, constant in composition, and not appreciably destructive to gelatine. Prepare potassium bromide solution: 1 ounce per 12 ounces of water; if solution is neutral or slightly alkaline, faintly acidify with hydrochloric acid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting gelatine quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Gelatine quality varies; different commercial specimens perform differently in emulsions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purchase several small samples, make trial emulsions with each, and stock the sample that gives the best results. If unwilling to test, use equal quantities of Nelson's No.1 and X opaque (as recommended by Captain Abney). For the given quantities, allow 1¼ ounces of gelatine to soak and melt (yielding about 6 ounces bulk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing proportions and preliminary preparation of emulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: Emulsion is prepared from solutions of silver nitrate and potassium bromide plus a dilute gelatine solution; heating and controlled addition are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take equal bulks of the silver nitrate and potassium bromide solutions, place them in a water bath to get hot. Prepare a large beaker with equal bulk of hot water and add ½ ounce of the gelatine solution to every 12 ounces of water. Heat all to approximately 180°F (about 82°C). During mixing, add a little bromide to the gelatine, then a little silver through a fine-orifice funnel, swirling the liquid; alternate bromide and silver until all is added. Keep bromide in excess while mixing (note: experienced workers sometimes prefer keeping silver in excess, per Captain Abney). A properly mixed emulsion appears orange/orange-red by transmitted light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boiling (stewing) the emulsion to develop grains and sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: After mixing, the emulsion must be held at boiling point to cause silver-bromide molecules to aggregate and for the emulsion to increase in sensitiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the well-mixed emulsion in the water bath at the boiling point for about forty-five minutes. Boiling accelerates processes that also occur more slowly in the cold; heat is a catalyst rather than the sole cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity and effect of excess potassium bromide on speed of sensitization
rubrics_metrics.description: A comparatively large excess of potassium bromide in the emulsion markedly speeds the development of maximum sensitiveness and the aggregation of silver-bromide particles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical results (given as example): 0.2 grain per ounce excess → no increase after six hours; 2.0 grains per ounce → about half an hour; 20.0 grains per ounce → seven minutes. Use sufficient excess bromide to obtain desired development time, mindful of overall recipe balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing which constituents cause sensitization
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental procedure showing that removing soluble salts prevents the emulsion changing on boiling, and that adding back potassium bromide (not niter) restores the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an emulsion is precipitated and washed free of potassium nitrate and excess bromide, boiling produces no change; adding potassium bromide back to such washed emulsion restores aggregation and sensitization. This shows the critical role of excess potassium bromide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of potassium bichromate + dilute HCl to precipitate gelatine and stop light sensitivity (daylight handling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Addition of a saturated cold solution of potassium bichromate and a few drops of dilute (1:8) hydrochloric acid liberates chromic acid which precipitates gelatine and destroys the action of light on silver bromide, allowing subsequent operations in daylight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add, for every 6 ounces of mixed emulsion, 1 ounce of saturated cold potassium bichromate, swirl, then add a few drops of the dilute HCl and set aside briefly. The precipitated gelatine carrying silver bromide will settle and the supernatant liquid can be poured off clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Washing and redissolving the precipitated emulsion (pellicle)
rubrics_metrics.description: After chromic precipitation, the pellicle must be washed free of coloring matter and soluble salts before redissolving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wash until wash water shows no trace of color; use fine muslin filter for large quantities or decantation for small. Then dissolve the pellicle in water by immersion in the water bath, add remaining gelatine, and make up with alcohol and water to the required final volume. Filter the reconstituted emulsion through a funnel containing a pellet of cotton wool to remove lumps before coating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final formulation/conditioning of emulsion before coating
rubrics_metrics.description: After redissolving and adding remaining gelatine, the emulsion is made up with alcohol and water to workable consistency and filtered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example quantities given in lecture: after redissolving, make up with 3 ounces of alcohol and water to 30 ounces for the quantities used. Always filter through cotton wool to ensure smoothness before coating plates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique for coating plates
rubrics_metrics.description: How to apply emulsion to glass plates to obtain an even, setting film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place plate on a small block of leveled wood; pour a small quantity of emulsion down a glass rod and spread over the plate by the rod held horizontally. Transfer the plate to a leveled slab of plate glass to allow the emulsion to set, then place in a drying box. Aim for thin, uniform coating. Plates made by this described process are of very good quality and suitable for landscape work, though not of the absolute highest sensitivity without further operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filtering the emulsion prior to coating
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove particulate matter and coagula to achieve even coatings and prevent defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pass emulsion through a funnel containing a pellet of cotton wool to filter before coating plates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common defects to avoid (ammonium bromide, pink fog, frilling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain materials and improper handling cause characteristic defects in plates (for example, pink fog and frilling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ammonium bromide because it decomposes to acidic products, alters bromine percentage, and has a destructive action on gelatine causing pink fog and probable frilling. Ensure gelatine is not damaged by harsh salts; control acidity and storage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing originals and positioning glass for vitrifiable pictures on glass
rubrics_metrics.description: Original drawings/images should be well executed on white or preferably bluish paper; glass sheets are cut to pattern and placed on the reverse side of the paper with the coated side contacting the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saturate the paper with petroleum to make it transparent and to fix outlines; work one panel at a time if panel is large. Place each glass sheet on the reverse side of the prepared paper so the coated face will contact the original during exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitizing solution composition for pictures on glass
rubrics_metrics.description: The sensitizing solution for vitrifiable image-making combines bichromate of ammonia and a sugar/starch binder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dissolve bichromate of ammonia in water until saturated. Dissolve 5 grammes of powdered dextrin or glucose in 100 grammes of water. Add 10% of the bichromate solution to the dextrin solution, mix and filter. Coat the glass with this solution as thinly and uniformly as possible (use two brushes to equalize).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drying the sensitized glass (temperature and arrangement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapid, controlled drying is required to fix the sensitizer without over-drying and to ensure reproducible exposures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a small hot chamber at 50–60°C (120–140°F). Lay sheets on a wire grating situated about 35 cm above the bottom; do not place sheets into the chamber before the required heat is reached. A few seconds suffice per sheet for the specified setup; arrange sheets where heat is less intense to dry evenly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure time guidance for pictures on glass (dependence on light and temperature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposure time varies with sunlight and temperature; under moderate sun and temperature it is short, in dull weather or low temperature it is much longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in fine cloudless weather at 16–18°C exposure may be 12–15 minutes; in dark weather 30–50 minutes. If temperature >25°C keep the sheets cool and less dried (otherwise they may metallize and ruin the reproduction). If temperature <5°C keep sheets warm and do not expose frames to open air; keep behind a glass window at about 14–18°C. The thickness/opacity of the original paper also affects exposure time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing exposure using vitrifiable color adhesion
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple practical test to assess whether exposure time is sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take out a test piece, apply vitrifiable color to the sensitive surface and observe adhesion: if the color adheres only slightly to the dark (shady) portions, the exposure was too long and must be recommenced; if the color adheres too well (even to light areas), exposure was insufficient and must be continued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development by vitrifiable color and removal of bichromate layer
rubrics_metrics.description: After exposure, the vitrifiable color powder is applied and the bichromate/glucose film is removed to allow enamelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the dark-room, lay the exposed sheets with sensitive side up and strew the vitrifiable color powder lightly with a brush; the powder adheres to shady parts, developing the image. Prepare a bath of wood-spirit (solvent) with 30–40 grammes of nitric acid per 1,000 grammes of wood-spirit, dip the prepared glass to remove the bichromate coating and separate the glucose/bichromate film. Renew the bath if it becomes yellowish. After this, retouching by hand and firing/enamelling proceed as in ordinary glass painting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of vitrifiable process to other substrates
rubrics_metrics.description: The same sensitizing and vitrification approach can be used on multiple polished substrates besides glass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process applies to marble, wood, stone, lava, canvas prepared for oil painting, earthenware, pure or enameled iron, etc., with the main difference that these objects are not dipped but have the liquid poured over them while inclined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus and method for preparing hydrogen sulphide from coal-gas
rubrics_metrics.description: A laboratory method for producing hydrogen sulphide (H2S) by passing coal-gas through boiling sulphur using a simple glass retort arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a retort containing about one pound of sulphur heated to boiling. Insert a bent glass tube perforated near the closed end so perforations dip into boiling sulphur; connect tube to the coal-gas supply via caoutchouc tubing. Connect retort neck to a wash bottle and to a receiving flask, then to an aspirator to draw the gas. Draw coal-gas through boiling sulphur; H2S formed is washed and collected. Other coal-gas constituents are not affected and do not interfere with precipitation of metallic sulphides; the product is sufficiently pure for ordinary analytical purposes.
